newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turks protest at inaction over mystery killing.
newsitem.headline: Turks protest at inaction over mystery killing.

text.p: Several thousand Turks protested on Friday at the government's failure to find the killers of a leading journalist in a four-year-old case spotlighted again by a scandal linking the security forces to mystery murders.
Demonstrators carried carnations to the spot in an Ankara street where investigative journalist Ugur Mumcu was blown up by a car bomb outside his house.
No one has been arrested in the case despite government promises to find the killers. Police say they have few leads.
"We condemn all officials who say it is the debt of the state to shed light on this bomb attack and then do nothing," leftist deputy Onder Sav told the protesters.

Theories over the identity of Mumcu's killers have been revived in a wave of accusations that officials directed far-right hit squads to kill political opponents, Kurdish activists and business rivals.
Mumcu, a columnist for the left-wing Cumhuriyet daily, often warned of the existence of shady far-right drug gangs within the corridors of power.
He was also a staunch secularist who angered Islamists.
His writings have had an eerie ring to them since a senior policeman and a mobster on the run from political murder charges died in the same car in a traffic accident last November.
A government MP who heads a Kurdish anti-rebel militia was also in the car. Guns and silencers were found in the wreckage.
Mumcu is the most famous of more than 1,300 people, many of them Kurds, who human rights activists say have died since 1992 in unsolved political killings.
"This matter could be solved if the political powers want," said MP Sav.

The Islamist-led government has raised the possibility of a probe into the suspicious death in 1993 of gendarmerie head Esref Bitlis, believed to have tried to crack down on organised crime cells in the security forces.
Justice Minister Sevket Kazan last week commended a recent report by a professor at Istanbul University that concluded sabotage was responsible for the aircraft crash that killed Bitlis.
Bitlis was also a key figure in the fight against Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) rebels.
The front page of the Milliyet daily printed the photographs of seven renowned Turkish intellectuals who were killed in mystery attacks, in the 1970s, '80s and '90s.
"It is shameful that the secret curtain over the death of countless intellectual and honourable people in 'mystery' killings has still not been raised," said Milliyet columnist Derya Sazak.
"Turkey has carried the shame of political murders for 20 years," he said.

Recent media and public fascination over the stream of killings has been stoked by accounts of a shady figure known by the codename "Green" who allegedly heads a death squad team in the mainly-Kurdish southeast.
Leftist MP Sinan Yerlikaya, who says he once saw Green in a police station, last week told a news conference of the fear which the bearded killer spread in the Kurdish province of Tunceli.
"When someone said the bearded one was coming, the children even started to cry," he said.
According to media reports, a note bearing the word "Green" was also found on the body of murdered casino entrepreneur Omer Lutfu Topal, who was gunned down in Istanbul last year.
